source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

In the bustling ER, a nurse hurried between bays, her clipboard tucked under an arm, while a doctor checked vitals at the triage desk. The waiting chairs were filled with anxious patients and their companions; gurneys lined the corridor, each draped with white sheets. A curtain was drawn around a patient who seemed in distress, his companion holding his hand.

The intercom crackled to life, registering clinical urgency: "Code blue on Bay 3," it announced. Nurses moved quickly, each with a task marked by wristbands and forms. The doctor approached the triage desk, marking the patient's condition as critical.

In the waiting area, a woman complained of being made to wait too long. "We've been here for hours!" she exclaimed. Triage nurse Sarah reassured her, noting down the complaint on a form, while other patients anxiously shifted in their chairs.

Bay 3 was now open; paramedics wheeled in another gurney. The doctor and nurses sprang into action, securing monitors and setting up IV drips. "Patient needs immediate attention," the intercom repeated.

The curtain around Bay 4 was drawn back, revealing a patient with a severe injury. The doctor examined him quickly, calling out instructions to the nurse who adjusted his position on the gurney. 

Meanwhile, at the triage desk, another patient's condition was being prioritized: "Systolic pressure dropping, possible cardiac event," announced one of the doctors into the intercom.

The ER continued its frantic rhythm, each moment a race against time as nurses and doctors moved swiftly between bays, ensuring that every patient received timely care.

A companion sat anxiously in a nearby chair, their expression mirroring the patient's distress. The room was alive with the hum of machines and the faint scent of antiseptic.
